verdict: Lend selectively to NABH-accredited multi-specialty hospitals and organised diagnostic chains in Chandigarh with CGHS/TPA receivables discipline; avoid single-specialty and doctor-dependent units.
title: Chandigarh Hospitals & Diagnostics: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
A hospital turns doctors, beds, equipment and consumables into billed episodes; a diagnostic lab turns samples into test reports. Cash arrives from three payers: cash/insurance patients, TPA/insurer settlements, and government schemes such as CGHS. **Chandigarh's private network is small and unusually well accredited: 21 CGHS-empanelled facilities, of which 10 are hospitals and 9 of those hold NABH accreditation [1].** That accreditation is your first filter, not a formality.

## Where value and cash sit
Value sits in occupancy, specialty mix and payer mix; cash sits in the gap between billing and TPA/CGHS realisation. **Hospitals carry heavy reinvestment needs for expansion and equipment upgradation [9], so capex is continuous and free cash is thin at small units.** Peer diagnostics show the pricing reality: average revenue per test at Rs 357, down 8.7% YoY, even as tests per patient rose 9.2% [7]. So when a proposal lands, check payer mix and days-in-receivable by payer; if TPA/CGHS receivables exceed the customer's own stated cycle, ask for the ageing and the last three settlement advices.

## What has changed now
Demand is holding: brokerages expect listed diagnostics majors to sustain volume growth through FY27 on stable pricing and B2C demand [4][6], and Aster DM reported Q4 operating EBITDA margin of 21.7% versus 19.3% [5]. **But doctor retention is the live risk — rating reports flag intense competition from organised chains and moderate-sized hospitals, with doctor retention critical [10].** Locally, GMSH-16 alone runs over 20,000 emergency footfall a month, sometimes 24,000 [3]; that is public-sector volume your private borrowers compete with on price. Chandigarh-specific financial data is thin — collect from customer.

## Who to pursue, how to grow safely
Pursue NABH-accredited multi-specialty hospitals with diversified specialties [9], organised diagnostic chains with B2C volume, and units adding CGHS empanelment [1]. Avoid single-doctor clinics and single-specialty units where one consultant's exit moves revenue. **Structure as a working-capital line sized to verified TPA/CGHS receivables plus a term loan matched to equipment life; take monthly receivable ageing, payer-wise collections and occupancy/test volumes.** Covenant a minimum NABH status and doctor-retention ratio; if either slips, ask for the consultant contract list.

## Early-warning signs
- Payer ageing stretching beyond the customer's stated cycle (monthly) -> freeze enhancement, seek settlement proof.
- Average revenue per test falling faster than volume rises (quarterly) -> reprice exposure, ask for payer mix.
- Senior consultant exits or NABH lapse (quarterly) -> review limit, seek replacement pipeline.
- Capex funded by short-term lines (quarterly) -> restructure to term debt or decline.
